context: The excerpt does not describe LeRobot’s evaluation of SO-100 or SO-101 robot arms, so it provides no arm-specific success rates, trial counts, task protocol, or success criterion. It does, however, outline general statistical guidance for pass-fail testing. Required sample size depends on the desired confidence level and target probability of success, using n = ln(1−CL) / ln(PS) when no failures occur across n trials. If failures are observed, the estimated minimum probability of success can instead be derived from the binomial cumulative distribution function using the number of successes m and independent trials n. The excerpt therefore supplies a general framework for reporting binary success outcomes, but not the particular protocol used by LeRobot. It also does not define what constitutes a successful manipulation or specify whether trials involve repeated grasping, pick-and-place, or another task.

context: The excerpt establishes that Clopper–Pearson limits are obtained by inverting exact binomial tail probabilities, using α/2 for a two-sided 100(1−α)% interval. For the requested zero-failure case, observe x=n successes in n trials. The exact one-sided 95% lower confidence bound is p_L = 0.05^(1/n). Requiring p_L ≥ 0.95 gives 0.05^(1/n) ≥ 0.95, or n ≥ ln(0.05)/ln(0.95) = 58.40, so 59 trials are required. This is the exact one-sided binomial result. The familiar rule of three approximates the requirement as 3/n ≤ 0.05, yielding 60 trials. If “95% confidence” means a two-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson interval, use α/2 = 0.025 for the lower endpoint: p_L = 0.025^(1/n). Then n ≥ ln(0.025)/ln(0.95) = 71.36, so 72 trials with zero failures are required. Thus, 59 is the exact one-sided answer; 72 is the conservative two-sided Clopper–Pearson answer.
